alt: A timeline shows crime fiction emerging as a genre in the mid-19th century, with texts such as Hamlet and The Rime of the Ancient Mariner before it. Every set text shares a significant crime that drives the narrative, consequences that shape the structure, and transgressions against national, social, religious or moral laws. The question is which elements a text uses, and to what effect.
caption: Many set texts predate crime fiction, so ask which elements each text uses.

alt: Three columns: post-2000 prose (When Will There Be Good News?, Atonement, or Kala from 2027), pre-1900 poetry (The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, or five poems by Crabbe, Browning and Wilde), and a further text (Oliver Twist, Hamlet, The Murder of Roger Ackroyd or Brighton Rock). A note says set texts must be unannotated.
caption: One post-2000 novel, one pre-1900 poetry text and one further text.

alt: Six grouped elements with examples: the crime and the criminal (Pinkie Brown, Browning’s speakers), detection and resolution (Poirot, Jackson Brodie, Ida Arnold), guilt and its aftermath (the Mariner, Briony, Claudius), victims and justice (Reading Gaol, Fagin), setting, structure and language (Dickens’s London, Greene’s Brighton, King’s Abbot), and society and audience.
caption: Six groups of elements, each illustrated from the set texts.

alt: Three linked steps for the unseen: identify the elements including what is withheld, analyse methods, and build an argument. Below, the original five-line poem is marked: the first two lines are public testimony to the magistrate and the rest is unspoken private guilt, with notes on the legal register as a mask, the withheld lantern, and the silence of the final short sentence.
caption: Identify, analyse, then argue: here, a crime of omission hidden behind true facts.

alt: A balance tips towards the guilty. On that side, both texts centre on a transgressor’s guilt, with victims seen through the narrator’s memory. On the other, Robbie has his own sections and the dead crew haunt the Mariner. The judgement is that both are shaped by guilt but question whether the guilty narrator can do justice to the victim.
caption: Argue the view, give the victims their weight, then judge.
